html:
This is the map's label for the forest peoples of the northern taiga, from the Baltic to beyond the Urals, between about 2000 BCE and 1200 CE. Most spoke Uralic languages, the family that includes Finnish, Estonian, Hungarian and the Sámi languages.

Life followed the forest and its waters. People hunted elk and reindeer, fished the lakes and rivers, trapped fur animals and gathered berries. They used skis and sledges in winter and boats in summer. Settlements were small and often moved with the seasons. Farming reached the southern edge slowly and never replaced hunting in the far north.

Over these three thousand years the groups under this label took shape as known peoples:

  • in the west, the ancestors of the Finns, Karelians and Estonians;
  • along the Volga and Kama, the Mari, Udmurts, Komi and Permians;
  • east of the Urals, the Khanty and Mansi;
  • one Ugric group, the Magyars, moved onto the steppe and in the 890s into Hungary.

From the 700s furs drew traders. Squirrel, sable and marten pelts flowed south to the Volga Bulgars and on to the Islamic world, which paid in silver. Later the cities of Kievan Rus' and Novgorod sent men north to collect furs as tribute, and Slavic farmers settled the southern forests. By 1200 much of this zone was being drawn into the Rus' states, though hunting and fishing went on as before in the north.
